content: Norovirus infection, also known as Norwalk virus infection, is the leading cause of acute gastroenteritis. Noroviruses are single-stranded RNA, non-enveloped viruses that are highly contagious. Transmission typically occurs through contaminated food or water, or by contact with contaminated surfaces. The infection causes symptoms such as diffuse, stabbing abdominal pain, nausea, watery diarrhea, and vomiting. There is no age or gender predisposition for developing norovirus infection. Risk factors include close contact with infected individuals, especially within the same household, poor food-handling hygiene, and consumption of contaminated shellfish or raw vegetables. Symptoms of norovirus infection usually begin 12 to 48 hours after exposure and last for 24 to 72 hours. Most patients recover completely without specific treatment, requiring only hydration, and do not experience long-term complications. However, young children, the elderly, and immunocompromised individuals are at higher risk for complications. In rare cases, the illness can be severe, particularly in these vulnerable populations. Laboratory findings are generally non-specific but may indicate dehydration, such as elevated blood urea nitrogen (BUN), creatinine, relative polycythemia, and metabolic alkalosis. Real-time PCR is the most effective diagnostic method for norovirus infection. Supportive care, including oral or intravenous fluid replacement to address dehydration and electrolyte imbalances, is the primary treatment. Anti-motility and anti-emetic agents may be used in adults for symptomatic relief, though their efficacy is controversial. Antimicrobial agents, including antivirals, are not recommended for treating norovirus infection. Preventive measures include avoiding exposure, proper handwashing, and safe food handling practices. There is no vaccine available for norovirus. The virus is resistant to temperature changes and can survive in up to 10 ppm chlorine, exceeding levels typically found in public water systems. Simple measures, such as proper handling of cold foods, strict handwashing after bathroom use and before food preparation, and paid sick leave, can significantly reduce foodborne transmission. Isolation of sick patients in healthcare facilities and environmental disinfection are also important. Norovirus was originally called the Norwalk agent after an outbreak in Norwalk, Ohio, in 1968. It was first visualized using electron microscopy in 1972. Noroviruses belong to the Caliciviridae family and are genetically diverse. The genus Norovirus includes several strains, such as Hawaii virus, Mexico virus, and Desert Shield virus, which are classified into five genogroups (GI, GII, GIII, GIV, and GV). The most common strain involved in large outbreaks is genogroup II, genotype 4. Noroviruses are highly contagious, with as few as 10 viral particles sufficient to cause disease. Transmission occurs via the fecal-oral route and peaks during the most severe symptomatic period, continuing up to three days after recovery. Immunity is not acquired after infection due to the existence of many strains. A non-functional FUT2 gene mutation has been associated with protection against common norovirus strains, as FUT2 is required for viral transport in the small intestine. Norovirus infection should be differentiated from other causes of infectious vomiting and diarrhea, including other viral gastroenteritis (e.g., sapovirus, adenovirus, rotavirus), bacterial gastroenteritis (e.g., Yersinia, Vibrio, Shigella, Salmonella, Escherichia coli), and parasitic infections (e.g., amebiasis, cryptosporidiosis). Norovirus is the leading cause of acute gastroenteritis and foodborne illness across all age groups in the United States, causing approximately 21 million cases annually. Symptoms of norovirus infection include malaise, fever, diffuse stabbing abdominal pain, diarrhea, vomiting, and anorexia. Parents of infected children may report irritability and reduced urine output (oliguria or anuria). Physical examination may reveal low-grade fever, tachycardia, abdominal tenderness, and signs of dehydration, such as reduced skin turgor, sunken fontanelles, sunken eyes, and dry mucous membranes. Severe cases may present with hypotension and altered mental status. Laboratory findings may include elevated inflammatory markers, hypokalemia, and chloride-sensitive metabolic alkalosis. Dehydration markers, such as relative polycythemia, elevated BUN, and elevated creatinine (indicating pre-renal acute kidney injury), may also be present. RT-qPCR is the optimal diagnostic test, while enzyme immunoassays have lower sensitivity. Norovirus is not typically cultured. Supportive care remains the cornerstone of treatment, focusing on oral or IV fluid replacement to address dehydration and electrolyte disturbances. Anti-motility and anti-emetic agents may be used for symptomatic relief in adults, though their efficacy is debated. Antimicrobial and antiviral agents are not recommended. Primary prevention relies on safe food and water practices, as well as proper hand hygiene. Noroviruses are resistant to temperature changes and can survive in chlorinated water. Preventive measures, such as proper food handling, handwashing, and paid sick leave, can significantly reduce transmission. Isolation of infected individuals and environmental disinfection are also critical. The CDC does not actively monitor norovirus outbreaks but collects data through the National Outbreak Reporting System (NORS) and CaliciNet, a network of public health and food regulatory laboratories that submit norovirus sequences from outbreaks to a national database.
